headline: Passed housing credit enhancement and TIF district orders for 205 Corporate Drive after public hearings
summary: The Council approved several consent agenda items, referred three financing orders to committee for first reading, and held public hearings on a credit enhancement agreement and a tax increment financing district for property at 205 Corporate Drive, both passing after debate. The Council also approved board appointments, a baseball field naming, and a fire chief appointment.
decisions: Approved minutes of prior Council and Committee meetings
Passed Order 26-246 authorizing sale of property at 10 Hersey Avenue to Hershey Rental LLC for $15,000
Passed Order 26-248 authorizing construction contract with Sargent Corporation for Penjajawoc Sewer I-95 Crossing Project
Passed Order 26-249 authorizing sole source contract with Coastal Traffic, Inc. for MioVision Cameras
Passed Order 26-250 authorizing collective bargaining agreement with Bangor Federation of Public Employees, Local 6071
Referred Order 26-251 authorizing $4,455,000 in General Obligation Bonds to Finance Committee for first reading on August 17, 2026
Referred Order 26-252 authorizing a $6,575,000 loan from Maine Municipal Bond Bank to Finance Committee for first reading on August 17, 2026
Referred Resolve 26-253 accepting up to $300,000 from MaineHousing with a $126,000 match for Project HOPE to Government Operations Committee for first reading on August 17, 2026
Passed amendment by substitution to Order 26-242 on credit enhancement agreement for 205 Corporate Drive, 8-1
Passed Order 26-242 as amended authorizing credit enhancement agreement with Bangor Housing Development Corporation for 205 Corporate Drive, 6-3
Passed Order 26-243 authorizing creation of a Tax Increment Financing District for affordable housing at 205 Corporate Drive, 6-3
Passed Order 26-247 appointing nominees to various boards and committees, 5-4
Passed Order 26-254 authorizing official naming of the baseball field at Mansfield Stadium in honor of Ronald J. St. Pierre, 9-0
Passed Order 26-255 authorizing City Manager's appointment of Eric Pelletier as Fire Chief, 9-0

is J. Good in, MMC, City Clerk

Good evening. My name is Teresa Fallon. I'm a mother of three, a person in recovery, a case manager, and a resident of Bangor.
I'm here tonight because my daughters, who are now nine and ten years old, have experienced racial discrimination in this
community for years. It began when my youngest daughter was only six years old.
My children have been called racial slurs and had insults made toward their skin and their hair. Recently, at summer camp, a
child would not passthe ball to my daughter and said," I'm not aliowed to touch Black people."
What I want to talk about is bigger than what has happened to my own children.
Discrimination takes on many forms— we discriminate based on the color of someone' s skin, whether they have a home,
whether they struggle with addiction, and even where someone was born.
These painful experiences do not just disappear when the moment is over. They leave a life- long impact.
Recently,avideowasmadeto discreditthe experiencesI havepubliclysharedabout mychildren.Thecreatorsof that video do
not deserve recognition from me. But I do want to saythis: when a parent speaks out about discrimination their child has
experienced— or when anyone expressesthat they have experienced discrimination— our response should not be to
immediately question, dismiss, or discredit their experience. it should be to listen.
I think we need to talk about where children learn these things.
Children are not born believing that someone is lessworthy because of the color of their skin. They are not born believing that
someone is less worthy because they are unhoused, strugg ing with addiction, poor, or simply different from them.
They learn it from us.
Theyhearthe conversationshappeningat home.Theyhearthe jokesandthe comments.Theyhearthe wayadultsspeakabout
peoplewho look different from them.Theyalsohearthe way adultsin this communityspeakabout peopleexperiencing
homelessness and substance use disorder right now.
Eventually, they repeat those things to other children. They begin to believe that our differences, our circumstances, or our
hardships make some people less dese"rving of dignity than others.
Adults and parents have to be willing to look at what we are teaching our children through the way we speak and behave.
My daughtersshouldnot havehad,to learnhowto respondto racismat sixyearsold.Theyshouldnot haveto wonderwhether
someone will make a comment about their skin or their hair when they walk into a new space. And no child should have to hear
someonethey lovereducedto a labelbecausetheyarestrugglingwith substanceusedisorderor homelessness.
I'mstandingherebecauseI believewecandobetter.
I want mydaughters—andeverychildin Bangor—to grow up knowingthat the adultsin their communitywill take
discriminationseriously,that we don't leavepeoplebehindbecauseof their hardships,andthat we arewillingto holdourselves
accountable for the environment we are creating for them.
Our children are learning from us.
And what we teach them today is the community they will create tomorrow.
Thank you.
